To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we introduce the first statistical framework for analyzing the sample size required for learning a clustering representation from a small sample of the data, and (2) we show that classes of representations induced via linear embeddings have finite capacity.

a) we introduce a novel protocol for incorporating domain knowledge in clustering; b) we provide a statistical framework to analyze the sample complexity of the protocol; and c) we show that linear embeddings can be successfully learned in our setting.

1) a clustering representation can be learned from sample, 2) the sample complexity is related to the capacity of the class of possible representations and 3) classes of linear representations have finite capacity, and hence can be successfully learned from sample.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a statistical framework for analyzing the sample and computational complexity of the problem of learning a representation for clustering.
the problem of designing clustering algorithms with the ability to incorporate user's domain knowledge.
the following question: How can a user communicate domain knowledge to the designer of an unsupervised learning algorithm?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our paper provides a statistical framework for representation learning in the context of clustering, and we show how this framework can be applied to the specific problem of learning a linear representation.

the proposed protocol can successfully learn a good representation from a small random sample of the data, if the representation class is sufficiently expressive, in the sense that it has finite capacity.
we have developed a framework for analyzing the sample size requirements for learning a representation for clustering.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a novel approach to the problem of clustering, which is based on learning a representation for the data that makes clustering easy.

we provide a theoretical framework for analyzing and understanding the sample complexity of the problem of learning a representation for clustering from a user's sample, and we show that this problem can be effectively solved for certain classes of representations.
we provide a theoretical framework for learning a representation that can be used to cluster data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, under a natural statistical model, the problem of learning a representation for a clustering problem is not fundamentally harder than the problem of learning the representation itself.

, in the context of learning representations for clustering, it is important to consider not only the sample size required for learning, but also the sample size required to communicate the user's knowledge of the underlying data distribution.

, in a setting where the user has a good idea of the underlying structure of the data, it is possible to learn a representation under which $K$-means can recover this structure, and to do so with small sample size.
